```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(ggplot2); library(clock)
  library(CDMConnector); library(PatientProfiles); library(OmopSketch)
})
source(file.path(Sys.getenv("WS_HOME", "/srv/workshop"), "app", "tutorial.R"))

# One participant per container: run exercises in this R process. learnr's default on Linux forks a
# child per exercise, which is not safe with DuckDB's threads.
options(tutorial.exercise.evaluator = learnr:::inline_evaluator)
# Tables in results: every column, in a box that scrolls (ws_print_table() in app/tutorial.R), not paged.
tutorial_options(exercise.timelimit = 300, exercise.completion = FALSE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(exercise.df_print = ws_print_table)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE)   # message = FALSE: no progress messages in results
# Show results wide enough that the interesting columns are not hidden as "... more variables", and keep
# OmopSketch's progress messages out of participants' results.
options(width = 160, cli.default_handler = function(...) NULL)
# Plots: large text, Hanze orange.
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 16))
update_geom_defaults("col", aes(fill = "#EE7F00"))
update_geom_defaults("bar", aes(fill = "#EE7F00"))

# The dataset: one shared DuckDB file, attached read-only (see ws_cdm() in app/tutorial.R).
# WS_RENDER_ONLY=1 while the image is built: there is no data then.
if (!nzchar(Sys.getenv("WS_RENDER_ONLY"))) cdm <- ws_cdm()
```

```{r cdm-guard, include=FALSE}
# Runs before every code box (each box has exercise.setup = "cdm-guard"): make sure `cdm` works, also if a
# participant broke it in an earlier box.
if (!nzchar(Sys.getenv("WS_RENDER_ONLY"))) cdm <- ws_cdm_ok(cdm)
```

```{r ws-assets}
ws_assets()
```

```{r ws-server, context="server"}
ws_server(session)
```

## Welcome

Welcome to this hands-on workshop! Hospitals and researchers around the world store health data in the same
way: the **OMOP Common Data Model**. Today you explore such a dataset yourself, with the programming language
**R**. No experience with R is needed: all code is ready for you, and you only change small pieces.

**Why R?**

R is a programming language for working with data and statistics. In the OHDSI community, the people around the
OMOP CDM, R is a *first-class citizen*: most of the community's open-source tools (such as the HADES packages for
cohorts, characterisation and prediction) are R packages, and so are the packages you use today (CDMConnector,
PatientProfiles and OmopSketch). What you learn here is how OMOP data is analysed in real studies.

**What you will do**

1. **Getting started**: a first look at the dataset.
2. **Counting people**: how many people, how many women and men, what the codes in the data mean, and how to
   turn codes into names.
3. **The concept hierarchy**: how medical terms are organised, like a family tree.
4. **Health records**: the most common diagnoses, medicines and procedures, and COVID-19 over time.
5. **Quick summaries**: ready-made summaries of a whole table, in one line of code (with the OmopSketch package).

**How this works**

- Every grey code box works the same way: press **Run Code**, and the result appears below it. You may change
  the code and run it again; **Start Over** puts the original code back.
- Some code boxes have a **blank**, `____`, for you to fill in. If you get stuck, press **Hint**.
- Questions are in boxes with an orange edge: fill in your answer and press **Save answer**. Later, your
  facilitator shows the feedback.
- The parts in the list on the left open one by one, when your facilitator is ready. You will see a message when
  that happens; you do not need to reload the page.

Your facilitator opens **1. Getting started** first. Until then, read this page and wait for the message.

## 1. Getting started

::: {.ws-section data-section="start"}

### 1.1 What is in this dataset?

In this workshop we look at a **synthetic** dataset: made up, but realistic, health records of about 10,000
people. It is stored in the **OMOP Common Data Model (CDM)**, a standard way of organising health data in
tables.

The data is ready for you under the name `cdm`. Press **Run Code** for an overview of the dataset.

```{r snapshot, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
summariseOmopSnapshot(cdm) |>
  tableOmopSnapshot()
```

What the code does:

- `summariseOmopSnapshot()` and `tableOmopSnapshot()` are **functions**: ready-made commands with a name followed
  by brackets. You put what they should work on between the brackets. These two come from the **OmopSketch**
  package: a collection of functions that others wrote for OMOP data, and that we have already loaded for you.
- `summariseOmopSnapshot(cdm)` collects facts about the dataset `cdm`: where it comes from, how many people are
  in it, the period it covers, and which versions it uses.
- `|>` means **"and then"**: it passes the result on to the next function.
- `tableOmopSnapshot()` shows those facts as a readable table.

```{r q-data-end}
ws_question("data_end_year")
```

```{r q-cdm-version}
ws_question("cdm_version")
```

### 1.2 Which tables are there?

The data is spread over many tables. This is the picture from the presentation: every box is a table, grouped
by what it holds, such as clinical data (people and their health records) and vocabularies (the codes and what
they mean).

```{r cdm-diagram}
# Served from this workshop's folder (not the internet). Source and licence: images/ATTRIBUTION.md.
htmltools::tags$figure(style = "margin-bottom: 1.6em;",
  htmltools::tags$img(src = "images/cdm-diagram-v6.png", style = "width: 100%; height: auto;",
                      alt = "Overview of the tables of the OMOP Common Data Model"),
  htmltools::tags$figcaption(style = "font-size: 14px; color: #5F6155; margin-top: 6px;", htmltools::HTML(paste0(
    "Overview of all tables in the CDM version 6.0. Our dataset uses version 5.3, so a few tables differ. ",
    "Source: Figure 4.1 of <em>The Book of OHDSI</em>, chapter 4 &ldquo;The Common Data Model&rdquo; ",
    "(chapter lead: Clair Blacketer), OHDSI, 2021, <a href=\"https://book.ohdsi.org\" target=\"_blank\">book.ohdsi.org</a>. ",
    "Licensed under <a href=\"https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/\" target=\"_blank\">CC0 1.0</a>."
  )))
)
```

The function `names()` lists the tables that are in our dataset:

```{r table-names, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
names(cdm)
```

In this workshop we use only a few of them: `person` and `death` (people), `condition_occurrence`,
`drug_exposure` and `procedure_occurrence` (health records), and `concept` and `concept_ancestor` (vocabularies).
Find them in the picture.

```{r q-vocab-group}
ws_question("vocab_group")
```

Now look at the result of `names(cdm)` again:

```{r q-concept-in-data}
ws_question("concept_in_data")
```

:::

## 2. Counting people

::: {.ws-section data-section="people"}

### 2.1 How many people are there?

In 1.2, `names(cdm)` showed the tables in `cdm`. You pick one table by its name with a `$`: `cdm$person` is the
table called `person`. The `person` table has **one row per person**, so if we count the rows, we count the
people.

```{r count-people, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$person |>
  count()
```

- `cdm$person` takes the `person` table from the data.
- `|>` means **"and then"**.
- `count()` is a function that counts the rows.

```{r q-n-people}
ws_question("n_people")
```

### 2.2 What is in the person table?

`head()` shows the first few rows of a table: a quick way to see which columns it has. The table is wider than
the screen: scroll sideways in the table (with the mouse wheel and Shift, a trackpad, or the scroll bar) to see
the other columns.

```{r person-head, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$person |>
  head()
```

Each row is a person. The columns describe that person, for example `gender_concept_id` (their gender) and
`year_of_birth`. Remember these columns: you need them in the next steps.

### 2.3 How many people per gender?

Now we count per gender. `group_by()` makes one group for every different value in a column; `count()` then
counts the rows in each group.

```{r gender-ids, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$person |>
  group_by(gender_concept_id) |>
  count()
```

The result has numbers such as 8507 and 8532 instead of names. These are **concept IDs**: codes. In the OMOP CDM,
almost everything is stored as a code like this.

### 2.4 Look up a code yourself

What does 8532 mean? Every code is described on **Athena**, the online dictionary of OMOP codes. Open
<https://athena.ohdsi.org> in a new tab, choose **Search**, type `8532` in the search box and press Enter. Click
the result to see its details.

```{r q-gender-8532}
ws_question("gender_8532")
```

Now you know which code is which, you can read the answer to this question from the result of 2.3:

```{r q-n-female}
ws_question("n_female")
```

### 2.5 Look up a code with R

The same information as on Athena is in the `concept` table of our data. `filter()` keeps only the rows we ask
for: here, the row where `concept_id` is 8532.

```{r gender-concept, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$concept |>
  filter(concept_id == 8532)
```

Now you: look up the **other** gender code from the result of 2.3. Fill it in, and press **Run Code**.

```{r gender-other, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$concept |>
  filter(concept_id == ____)
```

<div id="gender-other-hint">
**Hint:** the result of 2.3 has two codes: 8532, and one other. That is the one to fill in.
</div>

```{r q-gender-8507}
ws_question("gender_8507")
```

### 2.6 Fill in the blank: year of birth

`summarise()` calculates one number from a whole column. Here we want the **median** year of birth. Fill in the
name of the column that holds the year of birth (you saw it in 2.2), and press **Run Code**. (`na.rm = TRUE`
means: ignore people whose year of birth is missing.)

```{r median-birth, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$person |>
  summarise(median_year = median(____, na.rm = TRUE))
```

<div id="median-birth-hint">
**Hint:** look at the column names in the result of 2.2. One of them is about the year in which a person was
born.
</div>

```{r q-median-birth-year}
ws_question("median_birth_year")
```

### 2.7 A first plot: births per decade

A picture often says more than a number. This code puts everyone in the decade they were born in (1930, 1940,
...), counts the people per decade, and draws a bar for each decade.

> Do not worry about the code in this step: you do not need to write a plot yourself today. Press **Run Code** and
> look at the result; the list below the box is for those who are curious.

```{r birth-plot, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard", fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5}
cdm$person |>
  mutate(decade = floor(year_of_birth / 10) * 10) |>
  count(decade) |>
  collect() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Decade of birth", y = "People")
```

- `mutate()` adds a column: here `decade`, the year of birth rounded down to tens.
- `collect()` brings the result into R, so we can plot it.
- `ggplot()` starts a plot, `aes(x = decade, y = n)` says what goes on the axes, and `geom_col()` draws the bars.
  In a plot, the steps are joined with `+` instead of `|>`.

```{r q-birth-decade}
ws_question("birth_decade")
```

### 2.8 From codes to names

In 2.3 we counted per gender code, and in 2.4 and 2.5 we looked up the codes separately. We can also put the names
next to the codes in R, by **joining** two tables. `left_join()` keeps every row of the table on the left (our
counts) and adds the matching information from the table on the right (`concept`): for every row, it finds the
row in `concept` where `concept_id` is the same as our `gender_concept_id`.

```{r left-join-picture}
htmltools::tags$figure(style = "margin-bottom: 1.6em;",
  htmltools::tags$img(src = "images/left-join.svg", style = "width: 100%; max-width: 820px; height: auto;",
                      alt = paste("A left join: the counts per gender code on the left, the concept table on the right,",
                                  "and the result with the name of each code next to its count")),
  htmltools::tags$figcaption(style = "font-size: 14px; color: #5F6155; margin-top: 6px;",
    "A left join: every row on the left gets the matching columns from the right. Rows on the right without a match are left out.")
)
```

A join adds *all* the columns of `concept`, and we only need the name. `select()` keeps only the columns you list.

```{r gender-names, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$person |>
  group_by(gender_concept_id) |>
  count() |>
  left_join(cdm$concept, by = c("gender_concept_id" = "concept_id")) |>
  select(gender_concept_id, concept_name, n)
```

- `left_join(cdm$concept, by = c("gender_concept_id" = "concept_id"))`: join with `concept`, matching
  `gender_concept_id` in our counts to `concept_id` in `concept`.
- `select(gender_concept_id, concept_name, n)`: keep the code, its name and the count. Curious what the join
  brings without this step? Remove the last line (and the `|>` before it) and run the code again.

### 2.9 A shortcut: `addConceptName()`

Looking up names is so common that the **PatientProfiles** package has a shortcut for it. `addConceptName()` adds
the name for a code column; here we call the new column `gender`, and then count per gender. The result is the
same as in 2.8, with much less code.

```{r add-concept-name, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$person |>
  addConceptName(column = "gender_concept_id", nameStyle = "gender") |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  count()
```

### 2.10 Your turn: race

The `person` table also has a column with a code for each person's race. Use the shortcut from 2.9: fill in
the name of that column (look at the columns in 2.2), and count per race.

```{r race-names, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$person |>
  addConceptName(column = "____", nameStyle = "race") |>
  group_by(race) |>
  count()
```

<div id="race-names-hint">
**Hint:** in 2.9 the column was `gender_concept_id`. The column for race is named the same way.
</div>

```{r q-n-asian}
ws_question("n_asian")
```

:::

## 3. The concept hierarchy

::: {.ws-section data-section="hierarchy"}

Concepts are organised in a **hierarchy**, like a family tree: *atrial fibrillation* (a heart rhythm disorder)
is a kind of *atrial arrhythmia*, and *paroxysmal atrial fibrillation* is a kind of atrial fibrillation. In this
part you walk up and down that tree.

```{r hierarchy-picture}
htmltools::tags$figure(style = "margin-bottom: 1.6em;",
  htmltools::tags$img(src = "images/hierarchy-af.svg", style = "width: 100%; max-width: 820px; height: auto;",
                      alt = paste("Part of the concept hierarchy around atrial fibrillation: above it Atrial arrhythmia",
                                  "and Fibrillation, higher up Supraventricular arrhythmia and Cardiac arrhythmia, below it",
                                  "kinds of atrial fibrillation such as Paroxysmal and Persistent atrial fibrillation")),
  htmltools::tags$figcaption(style = "font-size: 14px; color: #5F6155; margin-top: 6px;", htmltools::HTML(paste0(
    "Part of the hierarchy around atrial fibrillation (not every concept is shown). Simplified from a figure in the ",
    "<a href=\"https://academy.ehden.eu/\" target=\"_blank\">EHDEN Academy</a>."
  )))
)
```

### 3.1 Find atrial fibrillation

First on Athena: search for `atrial fibrillation`. There are many results; we want the **condition** (the
diagnosis). On the left, choose **Domain: Condition** and **Standard concept: Standard**, and open the result
called *Atrial fibrillation*. The tab **Hierarchy** shows what is above and below it.

Now with R: find the concepts with exactly this name, in the domain *Condition*.

```{r af-find, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$concept |>
  filter(concept_name == "Atrial fibrillation", domain_id == "Condition")
```

There are two, from different **vocabularies** (coding systems: SNOMED and ICD9CM). The column
`standard_concept` shows an **S** for the one that OMOP uses as the standard (scroll sideways in the table to see
that column).

```{r q-af-concept-id}
ws_question("af_concept_id")
```

### 3.2 One step up

The `concept_ancestor` table links every concept to everything **above** it (its ancestors) and **below** it
(its descendants). `min_levels_of_separation == 1` means: only one step away. This code finds what is directly
above atrial fibrillation: rows where atrial fibrillation is the **descendant**. It then adds the names of the
**ancestors**. Fill in the concept ID of atrial fibrillation that you found in 3.1, and press **Run Code**.

```{r af-up, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$concept_ancestor |>
  filter(descendant_concept_id == ____, min_levels_of_separation == 1) |>
  addConceptName(column = "ancestor_concept_id", nameStyle = "name")
```

<div id="af-up-hint">
**Hint:** the concept ID from 3.1: the row for atrial fibrillation with an **S** in `standard_concept`.
</div>

```{r q-af-parent}
ws_question("af_parent")
```

### 3.3 Fill in the blank: one step down

Now the other way: what is directly **below** atrial fibrillation? This time atrial fibrillation must be the
**ancestor**. Fill in the column name in the first step.

```{r af-down, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$concept_ancestor |>
  filter(____ == 313217, min_levels_of_separation == 1) |>
  addConceptName(column = "descendant_concept_id", nameStyle = "name")
```

<div id="af-down-hint">
**Hint:** in 3.2 the first step used `descendant_concept_id`. Now atrial fibrillation is the ancestor: use the
other column, `ancestor_concept_id`.
</div>

```{r q-af-children}
ws_question("af_children")
```

**Bonus:** the result has more columns than we need. Add `select()` (from 2.8) to keep only the column with the
names.

```{r af-names, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$concept_ancestor |>
  filter(ancestor_concept_id == 313217, min_levels_of_separation == 1) |>
  addConceptName(column = "descendant_concept_id", nameStyle = "name") |>
  select(____)
```

<div id="af-names-hint">
**Hint:** `addConceptName()` put the names in a new column, and the code above gave it its name with
`nameStyle = "name"`.
</div>

```{r q-hierarchy}
ws_question("hierarchy_table")
```

:::

## 4. Health records

::: {.ws-section data-section="records"}

So far we looked at people and codes. Now the health records themselves: every diagnosis is a row in
`condition_occurrence`, every medicine or vaccination a row in `drug_exposure`, and every procedure (such as a
scan or an operation) a row in `procedure_occurrence`.

### 4.1 Fill in the blank: how many diagnoses?

Count the rows of the table with diagnoses. Fill in the function that counts rows: you used it in 2.1.

```{r count-conditions, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$condition_occurrence |>
  ____()
```

<div id="count-conditions-hint">
**Hint:** in 2.1, the function after `cdm$person |>` counted the people. Its name is a verb that means: tell how
many.
</div>

```{r q-n-conditions}
ws_question("n_conditions")
```

### 4.2 Fill in the blank: how often atrial fibrillation?

Each record has a `condition_concept_id`: the code of the diagnosis. Fill in the concept ID of atrial
fibrillation, which you found in part 3.

```{r count-af, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$condition_occurrence |>
  filter(condition_concept_id == ____) |>
  count()
```

<div id="count-af-hint">
**Hint:** it is the number in 3.2 and 3.3: the standard concept for atrial fibrillation.
</div>

```{r q-af-records}
ws_question("af_records")
```

### 4.3 The most common diagnoses

This code adds the name of each diagnosis, counts the records per name, and puts the largest first.
`collect()` brings the result into R, and `arrange(desc(n))` sorts it from high to low.

```{r top-conditions, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$condition_occurrence |>
  addConceptName(column = "condition_concept_id", nameStyle = "condition") |>
  count(condition) |>
  collect() |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

```{r q-top-condition}
ws_question("top_condition")
```

### 4.4 A plot: the top 10 diagnoses

The same counts, as a bar chart. `slice_max(n, n = 10)` keeps the 10 largest; `geom_col()` draws a bar for each.

```{r top-conditions-plot, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard", fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
cdm$condition_occurrence |>
  addConceptName(column = "condition_concept_id", nameStyle = "condition") |>
  count(condition) |>
  collect() |>
  slice_max(n, n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = reorder(condition, n))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Number of records", y = NULL)
```

```{r q-second-condition}
ws_question("second_condition")
```

Which table holds the drugs? `grep()` searches a list: here the table names from `names(cdm)`, for names with
"drug" in them.

```{r find-drug-table, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
grep("drug", names(cdm), value = TRUE)
```

There are three. `drug_exposure` holds the records themselves (`drug_era` and `drug_strength` are summaries and
reference data). Fill it in, and count its rows:

```{r count-drugs, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$____ |>

```

<div id="count-drugs-hint">
**Hint:** the table with the records is the first of the three: `drug_...`.
</div>

```{r q-drug-records}
ws_question("drug_records")
```

### 4.6 Fill in the blank: the most common drugs

The same as 4.3, but for drugs. First look at the columns of `drug_exposure`: `colnames()` lists the names of
the columns of a table.

```{r drug-columns, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
colnames(cdm$drug_exposure)
```

Fill in the column with the drug code:

```{r top-drugs, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}

  addConceptName(column = "____", nameStyle = "drug") |>
```

<div id="top-drugs-hint">

### 4.7 Find COVID-19

This dataset was made to study COVID-19. Find its concept ID, as you did for atrial fibrillation in 3.1. This
time we search for every condition with "COVID" in its name: `grepl()` checks whether a name contains a word.
`standard_concept == "S"` keeps only the standard concepts, and `select()` keeps only the ID and the name.

```{r covid-find, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
cdm$concept |>
  filter(grepl("COVID", concept_name), domain_id == "Condition", standard_concept == "S") |>
  select(concept_id, concept_name)
```

Several standard concepts mention COVID-19. Look for the one called exactly **COVID-19**.

```{r q-covid-concept-id}
ws_question("covid_concept_id")
```

### 4.8 A plot: COVID-19 over time

How many people were diagnosed with COVID-19, per month? `mutate()` adds a column: here `month`, the month of
each diagnosis. Then we count per month and draw a bar per month.

```{r covid-plot, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard", fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5}
cdm$condition_occurrence |>
  filter(condition_concept_id == 37311061) |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(condition_start_date, "month")) |>
  count(month) |>
  collect() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Diagnoses")
```

```{r q-covid-peak}
ws_question("covid_peak")
```


### 4.10 Fill in the blank: deaths

The `death` table has one row for every person who died. How many are there? By now you can write this yourself:

## 5. Quick summaries

::: {.ws-section data-section="omopsketch"}

In parts 2 to 4 you wrote the queries yourself. **OmopSketch** (<https://OHDSI.github.io/OmopSketch/>), the
package you used in 1.1, has ready-made summaries: one line of code for a table or a chart. This is how you
start with any new dataset.

### 5.1 Observation periods

The `observation_period` table says, per person, during which time their health records were collected.

```{r sketch-obs, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
summariseObservationPeriod(cdm$observation_period) |>
  tableObservationPeriod()
```

```{r q-obs-per-person}
ws_question("obs_per_person")
```

### 5.2 People in observation per year

How many people were observed in each year:

```{r sketch-trend, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard", fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
summariseTrend(cdm, episode = "observation_period", output = "person", interval = "years",
               dateRange = as.Date(c("2000-01-01", "2023-12-31"))) |>
  plotTrend()
```

```{r q-trend-2023}
ws_question("trend_2023")
```

### 5.3 The people, summarised

In part 2 you counted the people, the women and the men step by step. OmopSketch summarises the whole `person`
table in one line: sex, race, year of birth and more.

```{r sketch-person, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="cdm-guard"}
summarisePerson(cdm) |>
  tablePerson()
```

```{r q-sketch-women}
ws_question("sketch_women")
```

### To finish

```{r q-first-summary}
ws_question("first_summary")
```
